t: #2284 Sender With Largest Word Count — Editorial
o:
Each message is a space-separated word list with no leading/trailing spaces, so its word count is `count(' ') + 1`. Sum these per sender, then return the sender maximizing (word count, name) with lexicographically larger names winning ties.

Example 1: Alice sends 2 + 3 = 5 words and wins outright. Example 2: Bob and Charlie tie at 5, and 'Charlie' > 'Bob' lexicographically, so Charlie is returned.

With n ≤ 1e4 and messages ≤ 100 chars, a single hash-map pass is more than fast enough.
k: Word count of a message = number of spaces + 1 (guaranteed formatting).
Ties break toward the lexicographically largest sender name, so compare the tuple (count, name).

a.n: Approach 1: Single Pass with Hash Map
a.i: Accumulate word counts per sender in a dictionary, then select the max by (count, name).
s: For each message, add spaces+1 to its sender's tally.
Return the key maximizing (count, name) — in Python, max over items with key (cnt, name).
a.t: O(total characters) — one pass to count, one pass over distinct senders.
a.sp: O(number of distinct senders) for the map.

w: Straightforward; the only real decision is the tie-break comparison. Pitfall: comparing names with the wrong direction on ties (we want lexicographically LARGEST), and case sensitivity ('Alice' ≠ 'alice'). Follow-up: streaming version where messages arrive one at a time — the same map works incrementally.
